section.title: The Oracles of Balaam
section.sectionRationale: Having been restrained on the road, Balaam now stands before altars built at Balak's command and opens his mouth to curse Israel, but twice in a row only blessing comes out. This is the seam where the whole scheme against Israel collapses into open, poetic praise of the very God who is guiding the story.
section.thesis: Balak builds altar after altar, hoping a change of location will change the outcome, but Balaam's two oracles both declare that God is not a man who lies, that no spell or divination can touch Israel, and that God Himself has already spoken blessing that cannot be reversed.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the first oracle from the heights of Bamoth, declaring that God has not cursed what He has blessed; and the second oracle from the field of Zophim, declaring that God does not change His mind and that no curse can touch Israel.

units.label: The first oracle
units.note: how can I curse what God has not cursed

media.alt: Seven altars in a row on a barren height overlooking a distant camp
media.caption: Seven altars built, yet only blessing comes out of Balaam's mouth.

verses.text: Then Balaam said to Balak, “Build for me seven altars here, and prepare for me seven bulls and seven rams.”
So Balak did as Balaam had instructed, and Balak and Balaam offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
“Stay here by your burnt offering while I am gone,” Balaam said to Balak. “Perhaps the LORD will meet with me. And whatever He reveals to me, I will tell you.” So Balaam went off to a barren height,
and God met with him. “I have set up seven altars,” Balaam said, “and on each altar I have offered a bull and a ram.”
Then the LORD put a message in Balaam's mouth, saying, “Return to Balak and give him this message.”
So he returned to Balak, who was standing there beside his burnt offering, with all the princes of Moab.

And Balaam lifted up an {{oracle|oracle}}, saying: “Balak brought me from Aram, the king of Moab from the mountains of the east. ‘Come,’ he said, ‘put a curse on Jacob for me; come and denounce Israel!’
How can I curse what God has not cursed? How can I denounce what the LORD has not denounced?
For I see them from atop the rocky cliffs, and I watch them from the hills. Behold, a people dwelling apart, not reckoning themselves among the nations.
Who can count the dust of Jacob or number even a fourth of Israel? Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!”
Then Balak said to Balaam, “What have you done to me? I brought you here to curse my enemies, and behold, you have only blessed them!”
But Balaam replied, “Should I not speak exactly what the LORD puts in my mouth?”

units.label: The second oracle
units.note: God is not a man, that He should lie

verses.text: Then Balak said to him, “Please come with me to another place where you can see them. You will only see the outskirts of their camp, not all of them. And from there, curse them for me.”
So Balak took him to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah, where he built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
Balaam said to Balak, “Stay here beside your burnt offering while I meet the LORD over there.”
And the LORD met with Balaam and put a message in his mouth, saying, “Return to Balak and speak what I tell you.”
So he returned to Balak, who was standing there by his burnt offering with the princes of Moab. “What did the LORD say?” Balak asked.
Then Balaam lifted up an oracle, saying: “Arise, O Balak, and listen; give ear to me, O son of Zippor.
God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind. Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?
I have indeed received a command to {{bless|bless}}; He has blessed, and I cannot change it.
He considers no disaster for Jacob; He sees no trouble for Israel. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of the King is among them.
God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox.
For there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel. It will now be said of Jacob and Israel, ‘What great things God has done!’
Behold, the people rise like a lioness; they rouse themselves like a lion, not resting until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain.”
Now Balak said to Balaam, “Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!”
But Balaam replied, “Did I not tell you that whatever the LORD says, I must do?”
“Please come,” said Balak, “I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there.”
And Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the wasteland.
Then Balaam said, “Build for me seven altars here, and prepare for me seven bulls and seven rams.”
So Balak did as Balaam had instructed, and he offered a bull and a ram on each altar.

oracle.gloss: A weighty, elevated saying, often translated proverb or oracle. Balaam lifts up his mashal as formal, authoritative speech, marking these as no ordinary words but solemn declarations he insists come from God alone.

bless.gloss: To bless, to speak good and favor over someone. Balaam insists that once God has commanded barak, blessing, no human power, not even the one who received the order to curse, can reverse it, echoing God's unchanging character in verse 19.

basic.context: Balak keeps moving Balaam to new locations, hoping a different vantage point will produce a different result, but each time Balaam opens his mouth to curse Israel, only blessing comes out. These two oracles are some of the most theologically rich poetry in the Torah, declaring that God's word cannot be reversed by any human effort.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, historical confrontation between a pagan king's scheme and God's unbreakable purpose, told through solemn poetic oracles rather than plain narrative. The point is not primarily about Balaam's character, which remains ambiguous, but about the reliability of God's spoken blessing.
basic.originalLanguages: Balaam lifts up his mashal, a weighty oracle, insisting three times that he can only speak what the LORD puts in his mouth. His second oracle declares that God has received a command to barak, bless, and cannot reverse it, grounding Israel's security not in their own merit but in God's own unchanging word.
basic.typology: Verse 19, God is not a man, that He should lie, becomes a foundational statement about God's character quoted directly in later Scripture, and it anticipates the New Testament's confidence that God's promises in Christ are equally unbreakable, since it is impossible for God to lie, Hebrews 6:18.
basic.christ: While these oracles do not name a coming Messiah directly, they establish the theological bedrock the next chapter's messianic oracle stands on: God's blessing, once spoken, cannot be undone by any power. That same unbreakable reliability of God's word underlies every promise fulfilled in Christ, in whom all God's promises are yes and amen, 2 Corinthians 1:20.
basic.god: God is utterly unlike fickle human speakers; He does not lie, does not change His mind, and does not fail to keep His promises. His faithfulness to His own spoken blessing holds firm even when the person carrying that blessing, Balaam himself, is far from wholly faithful.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 6:22-27 recalls the priestly blessing God gave Israel, the very blessing Balaam here finds unable to reverse. Hebrews 6:17-18 grounds Christian assurance in the same truth stated in verse 19, that it is impossible for God to lie. Romans 11:29 echoes the principle that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable.
basic.oneStory: God's spoken blessing cannot be undone by any human scheme, however well-funded or well-intentioned, because God is not a man who lies or changes His mind. This unbreakable reliability of God's word, first proven here against a king's hired curse, is the same reliability that secures every believer's standing in Christ, in whom every promise of God finds its yes.

context.literary:
Numbers 23 is built from two cycles that run in close parallel, and the repetition is the point. Each cycle has the same steps: seven altars are built, a bull and a ram are offered on each, Balak is told to stand beside his offering, Balaam goes aside to meet the LORD, the LORD puts a word in his mouth, Balaam returns and lifts up an oracle, Balak protests, and Balaam replies that he can say only what the LORD gives. Compare verses 1 to 12 with verses 13 to 26. The chapter ends by starting a third cycle, verses 27 to 30, so that the reader expects the same result before it comes.

Within the pattern there is escalation. The first oracle, verses 7 to 10, is about Israel: its separateness and its countless number. The second, verses 18 to 24, is about God: His truthfulness, His presence as King among His people, and His power in bringing them out of Egypt. The movement is from what Balaam sees to why it is so.

Balak's protests shrink as the oracles grow. First he complains, 'What have you done to me?' verse 11. Then he gives up on cursing altogether: 'Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!' verse 25. Yet he cannot stop, and he tries a third time.

The oracles themselves are Hebrew poetry built on parallel lines, and nearly every couplet pairs Jacob with Israel: 'curse Jacob,' 'denounce Israel,' verse 7; 'no disaster for Jacob,' 'no trouble for Israel,' verse 21; 'no spell against Jacob,' 'no divination against Israel,' verse 23. The two names of the patriarch become a refrain of identity.

There is a verbal frame in the second oracle. It begins with a command to Balak, 'Arise,' verse 18, and ends with Israel who 'rise like a lioness,' verse 24. The king of Moab is told to get up and listen; the people he wanted cursed are the ones who rise.
context.historical:
The three hilltops chosen by Balak lie on the edge of the plateau above the plains of Moab. Bamoth-baal, 22:41, was a place of Baal worship. The field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah, verse 14, has a name meaning 'watchers' or 'lookouts,' a natural site for surveying the camp below, and Pisgah is where Moses will later view the land, Deuteronomy 34:1. Peor, verse 28, overlooks the wasteland, and its god, Baal of Peor, will be the snare of chapter 25.

The choice of places reflects a widespread ancient belief that a curse had to be spoken in sight of its target. Balak's instruction, 'come with me to another place where you can see them,' verse 13, assumes that the right view might yield the right result. Seeing only 'the outskirts of their camp' may have been meant to limit Balaam's sense of Israel's size, after the first oracle marvelled at their number, verse 10.

The sacrifices are lavish. Seven altars with a bull and a ram on each makes fourteen animals at each site, and the number seven carried the sense of completeness in rituals across the ancient Near East. Scripture records the same offering of seven bulls and seven rams in Job 42:8 and 1 Chronicles 15:26, but here it is put to the service of divination. Balaam's going off alone to 'a barren height,' verse 3, fits the practice of seeking omens, which Numbers 24:1 says he had done 'on previous occasions.'

The first hearers would have noticed how the oracles overturn the assumptions of that world. Balak believed gods could be moved by gifts and a curse could be steered by technique. Balaam, a professional in exactly that world, is made to announce that 'there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel,' verse 23.
context.canonical:
The central claim of the second oracle, that 'God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind,' verse 19, is echoed almost word for word by Samuel when God rejects Saul: 'the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind,' 1 Samuel 15:29. It becomes a fixed point in Scripture's teaching about God. Malachi 3:6 says, 'I, the LORD, do not change,' and draws the same conclusion: 'you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed.' Paul speaks of 'God, who cannot lie,' Titus 1:2, and Hebrews grounds Christian hope on 'two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie,' Hebrews 6:18.

The picture of Israel as 'a people dwelling apart,' verse 9, returns at the end of Deuteronomy: 'So Israel dwells securely; the fountain of Jacob lives untroubled,' Deuteronomy 33:28, in the blessing of Moses that mirrors Balaam's. Moses himself had asked how Israel would be 'distinguished from all the other people on the face of the earth,' Exodus 33:16, and answered that it would be by God's presence.

The image of the lion in verse 24 draws on Jacob's blessing of Judah, 'Like a lion he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?' Genesis 49:9, which Numbers 24:9 will quote almost exactly. Revelation 5:5 brings that line to its goal in 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah.'

The whole episode becomes a proof text of God's covenant love. Deuteronomy 23:5 says the LORD 'turned the curse into a blessing,' Nehemiah 13:2 repeats it, and Micah 6:5 calls Israel to remember what Balaam answered. Paul's words, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' Romans 8:31, could stand as a summary of this chapter.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The chapter was written to show Israel why they were safe. It was not their righteousness, their military strength, or their piety, since they did not even know the danger. It was the character of God. The heart of the chapter is verse 19, and the argument runs from God's nature to Israel's security: God does not lie, so His word of blessing stands; He does not change His mind, so no amount of sacrifice or relocation will move Him.

Moses also wanted Israel to hear their identity from an outsider. A foreign seer, hired to curse them, is made to say that they are separate from the nations, countless as dust, righteous, protected, led by a King in their midst, and brought out of Egypt by God. Israel had often forgotten who they were. Here the enemy's own prophet is made to remind them.

Finally, the chapter warns against a certain kind of religion. Balak and Balaam go through elaborate rituals, and nothing comes of them but what God had already said. The first hearers, soon to settle among peoples whose worship was built on such techniques, were to learn that God is not managed by ritual. He is to be trusted and obeyed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The altars, sacrifices and hilltop consultations are described, not commanded. They are the apparatus of divination, which the law forbids in Deuteronomy 18:10-12, and nothing in the chapter suggests God approved of them. He spoke in spite of them, not because of them.

The oracles themselves, though spoken by a compromised man, are presented as God's word: 'the LORD put a message in Balaam's mouth,' verse 5. Their content is therefore true and binding. Verse 19 is quoted and relied on elsewhere in Scripture as a statement about God.

For believers now, the chapter prescribes confidence rather than technique. Christians do not seek God's favour through ritual or by finding the right place or method. They rest on His word, which Hebrews 6:18 grounds in His inability to lie. The chapter also cautions against assuming that because someone speaks true words about God, he is himself right with God, as Balaam's later story shows.

debates.question: Why does Balak keep moving Balaam to new locations for each oracle?

views.label: A belief that a curse must be spoken in sight of its target
views.case: Ancient cursing assumed a line of sight between the curser and the cursed. Balak says 'come with me to another place where you can see them,' verse 13, and each hilltop overlooks the camp, 22:41 and 23:28. On this reading, the moves are ritual technique.

views.label: An attempt to limit what Balaam sees
views.case: After the first oracle marvels at Israel's numbers, verse 10, Balak takes him where he will 'only see the outskirts of their camp,' verse 13, as if a smaller view might produce a smaller blessing. The change of place is tactical.

views.label: A hope of finding a more favourable god or shrine
views.case: The sites include Bamoth-baal and Peor, places of local worship. Balak's words, 'Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there,' verse 27, suggest he thought divine favour might vary by place.

debates.bearing: The views overlap, and all rest on the same mistake: that God's word depends on circumstances. Verse 19 answers them all. A God who does not change His mind is not moved by a change of scenery, and the third move fails as surely as the first two.

debates.question: Does verse 21 mean that God sees no sin in Israel?

views.label: God sees no disaster coming for Israel
views.case: The BSB renders the words as 'disaster' and 'trouble,' reading the verse as a statement of Israel's protection: God has planned no harm against them, which is why no curse can land. This fits the context of blessing and curse and the next line about the King among them.

views.label: God does not count Israel's iniquity against them
views.case: The two Hebrew nouns can also mean 'iniquity' and 'wickedness,' and older translations read 'He has not beheld iniquity in Jacob.' On this reading the verse is about grace: God does not reckon Israel's sin in a way that would open them to Balak's curse, much like Romans 4:7-8 and Romans 8:1.

debates.bearing: The words carry both senses, and the two readings are closer than they seem. Israel was far from sinless, as Peor shows in chapter 25. What the oracle affirms is that God has not set Himself against them, so no disaster is planned. That is true only because He deals with their sin in mercy. The New Testament states the same reality in Christ: 'Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies,' Romans 8:33.

study.originalLanguages:
The first oracle turns on three verbs for cursing. Balak's request, as Balaam reports it, uses arar, 'put a curse on Jacob,' and za'am, 'denounce Israel,' verse 7. Za'am is a word for angry indignation, used elsewhere of God Himself, as in Malachi 1:4, 'a people with whom the LORD is indignant forever.' Balaam's answer in verse 8 switches to qabab: 'How can I curse what God has not cursed? How can I denounce what the LORD has not denounced?' The argument is that curses are only effective if God stands behind them. A curser has no power of his own. He can only echo what God has said.

Verse 9 calls Israel 'a people dwelling apart,' using the word badad, alone or isolated. The same word appears in Deuteronomy 33:28, where Moses blesses Israel as one who 'dwells securely,' and in Jeremiah 49:31, of a nation that lives 'alone,' without gates or bars. The phrase 'not reckoning themselves among the nations' uses the verb chashav, to count or reckon, the same verb Genesis 15:6 uses when Abram's faith 'was credited to him as righteousness.' Israel's separateness is not self-assessment but a status God assigned.

In verse 10 Balaam longs to 'die the death of the righteous,' yesharim, the upright. It is a plural of yashar, straight or upright, and it shares its root with Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel used in Deuteronomy 32:15, Deuteronomy 33:5 and 33:26 and Isaiah 44:2. Balaam, in effect, calls Israel by its honour name. The tragic irony is that he dies by the sword among Israel's enemies, Numbers 31:8.

Verse 19 is the theological centre. 'God is not a man,' ish, 'that He should lie, or a son of man,' ben adam, 'that He should change His mind.' The two terms for humanity span the whole human race. The verb 'lie' is kazav, to deceive or fail, and a related form describes 'a spring whose waters never fail,' Isaiah 58:11; the verb 'change His mind' is nacham, which elsewhere is translated 'relented' or 'regretted.' Exodus 32:14 says 'the LORD relented' and Jonah 3:10 that 'He relented from the disaster,' both using nacham. The two statements do not contradict each other. God does not reverse His purposes the way humans do, from fickleness or deceit; but He responds as He has said He will respond, Jeremiah 18:7-10, and those responses are themselves part of His unchanging character.

Verse 21 contains two words with a double edge. The BSB's 'disaster' is aven, which can mean trouble, iniquity or wickedness; 'trouble' is amal, which can mean toil, misery or mischief. The line can be read either as God seeing no harm for Israel or as God not beholding iniquity in them. The following line, 'the shout of the King is among them,' uses teru'ah, the word for the trumpet blasts sounded in battle, Numbers 10:9, and in worship, Leviticus 23:24. It is the acclamation of a king present with His army.

Verse 23 offers a pun. 'There is no spell against Jacob' uses nachash, a noun for omen or enchantment that shares its letters with nachash, serpent. Genesis 44:5 uses the related verb for Joseph's cup of divination. The preposition can be rendered 'against' or 'in': no omen works against Jacob, and none is needed in Jacob, because God speaks to His people directly. The verse ends with Israel's true oracle: 'What great things God has done!'

Finally, the two lions of verse 24 are labi, a lioness, and ari, a lion. The same pair appears in Jacob's blessing of Judah, Genesis 49:9, and will return in Numbers 24:9, where the quotation of Genesis becomes nearly exact.

typology.type: God who does not lie or change His mind, verse 19
typology.fulfillment: Balaam's oracle establishes the ground on which every later promise stands. Hebrews takes it up directly: God guaranteed His promise with an oath so that 'by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie,' we might be strongly encouraged, Hebrews 6:17-18. In Christ this reliability takes a human face: 'all the promises of God are "Yes" in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20, and 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever,' Hebrews 13:8. The escalation is that God's unchanging word is no longer only spoken over His people; it has become flesh and dwelt among them, John 1:14.

Israel was set apart among the nations, not by merit but by God's presence with them, Exodus 33:16. The church inherits the same identity: 'a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession,' 1 Peter 2:9. Jesus prays for His disciples as those who are 'not of the world, just as I am not of the world,' John 17:14-16, yet sends them into it. The type is fulfilled with a difference: Israel's separateness was partly ethnic and territorial, while in Christ the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile is torn down, Ephesians 2:14, and a new people is drawn from every nation.

typology.type: The King's shout among His people, verse 21
typology.fulfillment: The LORD is pictured as King present in Israel's camp, acclaimed with the battle shout, as when the ark set out and Moses cried 'Rise up, O LORD!' Numbers 10:35. The fulfilment comes when God comes among His people in person: 'they will call Him Immanuel,' which means 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23. Zephaniah 3:17 already looked ahead: 'The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save.' The type falls short in that the LORD was present in Israel through the ark and the cloud; in Christ He dwells among His people in flesh, and then by His Spirit within them.

Balaam pictures Israel rising like a lioness and a lion, drawing on the blessing of Judah in Genesis 49:9. That image narrows over time from the people to their king. Revelation 5:5 announces 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David,' who 'has triumphed.' Yet when John looks, he sees 'a Lamb who appeared to have been slain,' Revelation 5:6. The escalation is in the reversal: the lion's victory in Numbers comes by devouring prey, but Christ's victory comes through His own death.

study.christ:
These oracles lead to Christ first through their central claim about God's word. Balaam insists again and again that he can speak only 'the word that God puts in my mouth,' 22:38, and 'exactly what the LORD puts in my mouth,' 23:12. The phrase recalls God's promise in Deuteronomy 18:18: 'I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in his mouth.' Balaam is a compelled, reluctant mouthpiece. Jesus is the willing, perfect one: 'I have not spoken on My own, but the Father who sent Me has commanded Me what to say and how to say it,' John 12:49. The contrast is sharp. Balaam speaks God's words against his own desire; Christ speaks them because they are His delight.

They lead to Christ through the certainty of God's promise. Verse 19 establishes that God's word does not fail. That certainty is what makes every messianic promise trustworthy. 'For all the promises of God are "Yes" in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20. The blessing Balaam could not reverse, verse 20, is the blessing of Abraham, which Paul says comes to the nations 'in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:14.

They lead to Christ through the righteousness that shields God's people. Whether verse 21 is read as God seeing no disaster for Israel or no iniquity in them, it rests on the fact that God has not set Himself against them. In the New Testament that status belongs to those in Christ. 'There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,' Romans 8:1. The reason is not that believers are sinless, but that 'Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God,' 1 Peter 3:18. Christ is 'the Righteous One,' 1 John 2:1, Acts 3:14.

Balaam's wish, 'Let me die the death of the righteous,' verse 10, gains a new depth in this light. He longed for their end without sharing their God. The New Testament shows the way to die the death of the righteous: 'Blessed are the dead, those who die in the Lord,' Revelation 14:13, and 'to die is gain,' Philippians 1:21. The death of the righteous is secure only through the death of the Righteous One.

They lead to Christ through the King among His people. 'The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of the King is among them,' verse 21. Matthew opens his Gospel by announcing a child who will be called 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23, and closes it with the risen King's promise, 'surely I am with you always,' Matthew 28:20. The acclaimed King of verse 21 is fully revealed in Jesus.

Finally, the lion of verse 24 anticipates the Lion of Judah, Revelation 5:5. The oracle pictures Israel devouring its enemies. Revelation shows the King whose triumph is His own sacrifice, the Lion who is a Lamb.

Caution matters. Balaam was no Christian prophet, and the second oracle does not describe the Messiah in detail. What these verses supply is the foundation for the messianic oracle of chapter 24: a God whose word cannot fail, a people He will not curse, and a King already in their midst.
study.god:
The second oracle contains one of the clearest statements about God's character anywhere in the Old Testament. 'God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind. Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?' verse 19. The chapter shows what that means in practice.

God is truthful. His words match reality and will always match it. Balak hoped a curse spoken by the right person in the right place would change Israel's destiny. But curses only work if they agree with God's own word, verse 8, and God had already said, 'they are blessed,' 22:12. Human words have no independent power over His purposes. 'The counsel of the LORD stands forever,' Psalm 33:11.

God is faithful to what He has spoken. Verse 20, 'He has blessed, and I cannot change it,' shows that God's blessing is not a mood but a commitment. Isaiah 55:11 says His word 'will not return to Me empty.' This does not mean God is mechanical. Scripture also records that He 'relented,' Exodus 32:14, and that He responds to repentance, Jeremiah 18:7-10. But His responses flow from His settled character, not from a change of heart. What never changes is His covenant purpose.

God is sovereign over rival powers. The oracles declare that 'there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel,' verse 23. The whole machinery of ancient religion is powerless against Him. Isaiah later says the LORD 'foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners,' Isaiah 44:25. In the New Testament the same pattern recurs when sorcerers like Simon and Elymas are confronted by the word of God, Acts 8:9-11 and 13:6-12.

God is present with His people as King. 'The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of the King is among them,' verse 21. The line looks back to the song at the sea, 'The LORD will reign forever and ever,' Exodus 15:18, and forward to Deuteronomy 33:5, where 'the LORD became King in Jeshurun.'

God is a redeemer. 'God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox,' verse 22. The oracle roots Israel's security in the exodus. God's present protection is grounded in what He has already done.

The chapter holds a tension that careful readers feel. The God who does not change His mind nonetheless lets Balaam go through elaborate rituals and allows Balak to try again and again. He does not stop the scheme at the first attempt. He lets it fail publicly, three times, so that His faithfulness is seen. God's patience with His enemies becomes the stage on which His truthfulness is displayed.

For worship, the chapter invites believers to stand on the character of God. The Christian hope is not built on circumstances, feelings or technique, but on the God who 'cannot deny Himself,' 2 Timothy 2:13. And it gives words for praise: 'What great things God has done!' verse 23.

crossReferences.note: Samuel tells Saul that 'the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind.' The wording closely echoes Numbers 23:19, and it is applied now to God's judgment rather than His blessing. His word stands either way.

God confirmed His promise with an oath, so that 'by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie' believers may take hold of hope. Hebrews draws on the truth Numbers 23:19 states, that God's word and purpose do not waver, and makes it the anchor of Christian assurance.

Paul speaks of 'the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began.' The confession of Numbers 23:19 is carried into the New Testament as a fixed attribute of God and made the basis of the promise of eternal life.

'I, the LORD, do not change; you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed.' Like Numbers 23:19-20, Malachi ties Israel's survival to God's unchanging character. They have not been consumed, not because they deserved mercy, but because God stays true to His word.

In Moses' final blessing, 'Israel dwells securely; the fountain of Jacob lives untroubled in a land of grain and new wine.' The picture of a people living apart and secure, Numbers 23:9, becomes a blessing spoken by Israel's own prophet at the end of his life.

Moses asks how Israel will be 'distinguished from all the other people on the face of the earth, unless You go with us.' Numbers 23:9 describes a people 'dwelling apart,' and 23:21 gives the reason: 'The LORD their God is with them.' God's presence is what sets them apart.

Jacob's blessing of Judah, 'Like a lion he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?' supplies the imagery of Numbers 23:24. Balaam applies Judah's lion image to all Israel, and Numbers 24:9 will quote Genesis 49:9 almost exactly.

The Lion of the tribe of Judah has triumphed, yet John sees 'a Lamb who appeared to have been slain.' The rising lion of Numbers 23:24 finds its fullest meaning in a King whose victory comes through His own death, not through devouring His enemies.

The LORD 'foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners' and confirms the word of His servants. Numbers 23:23, 'there is no spell against Jacob,' is a historical instance of what Isaiah states as a principle of God's dealings with the nations.

God promises a prophet like Moses and says, 'I will put My words in his mouth.' Balaam uses the same language of God putting a message in his mouth, Numbers 23:5, 12 and 16. The compelled diviner is a dark foil for the true Prophet who speaks God's words willingly.

'If God is for us, who can be against us?' and 'Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies.' Paul's argument runs parallel to Balaam's: no one can curse or accuse those God has blessed. Numbers 23:8 and 23:20 are this truth in narrative.

The child is called Immanuel, 'God with us.' Numbers 23:21 announces that 'the LORD their God is with them, and the shout of the King is among them.' What Balaam saw in the camp of Israel, God fulfilled by coming among His people in the person of His Son.

'All the promises of God are "Yes" in Christ.' Numbers 23:19 asks, 'Does He promise and not fulfill?' Paul answers that every promise finds its fulfilment in Christ, the final proof that God's word does not fail.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers the oldest question in the Bible: can God's word be trusted? In Genesis 3 the serpent's first move was to cast doubt on what God had said, 'Did God really say?' and then to contradict it, 'You will not surely die.' Humanity's fall began with doubting God's word. Numbers 23 is a direct reply, spoken by an unlikely voice: 'God is not a man, that He should lie.'

It also answers the promise to Abraham. God had promised offspring like the dust of the earth, Genesis 13:16, and a blessing that would reach all nations. Balaam, standing on a hilltop in Moab, looks down and says, 'Who can count the dust of Jacob?' verse 10. The promise has been kept in visible form. And the blessing cannot be reversed, because 'He has blessed, and I cannot change it,' verse 20.

What follows sets up a tension that runs through the rest of the Old Testament. God's word of blessing stands, but Israel does not always live in it. In chapter 25 Israel falls at Peor. The people God will not curse bring judgment on themselves. From here to the exile, Israel's history is a long struggle between God's faithful word and the people's unfaithfulness. God keeps His promises, but the people keep breaking theirs.

That tension is resolved in Christ. He is the true Israel, the Righteous One whose death is truly 'the death of the righteous.' He fulfils every promise, 2 Corinthians 1:20, and He takes the curse Balaam could not pronounce, becoming 'a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, so that the blessing of Abraham reaches the nations. God's unchanging word, which once shielded Israel on the plains of Moab, now secures every believer in Christ. 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' Romans 8:31.

The story ends in the new creation, where God's truthfulness is vindicated forever. There God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3, as the King whose shout was once heard in Israel's camp. There is 'no longer any curse,' Revelation 22:3. Every word God has spoken will have been fulfilled, and His people will say with Balaam, but with full understanding, 'What great things God has done!'

quiz.q: What did Balaam do before receiving each of his two oracles in this chapter?

options.text: He had Balak build seven altars and offer a bull and a ram on each one.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 and 14 both describe this same preparation before each oracle.

options.text: He fasted alone for seven days in the wilderness.
options.note: The text describes altar-building and sacrifice, not a fasting ritual.

options.text: He consulted written omens brought from his homeland.
options.note: The preparation described is sacrificial, seven altars and offerings, not written omens.

options.text: No preparation is described before the oracles.
options.note: Verses 1 to 4 and 14 describe specific preparations in detail.

quiz.q: What was the outcome of Balaam's first oracle, according to verse 11?

options.text: Balak was furious because Balaam had only blessed Israel instead of cursing them.
options.note: Verse 11 records Balak's exact complaint.

options.text: Balak was pleased because Balaam successfully cursed Israel.
options.note: The opposite occurred; Balaam blessed rather than cursed Israel.

options.text: Balaam refused to speak at all.
options.note: Balaam did speak, delivering a full oracle of blessing rather than staying silent.

options.text: No reaction from Balak is recorded.
options.note: Verse 11 records Balak's clear and immediate reaction.

quiz.q: According to verse 19, what does Balaam's second oracle say about God's character?

options.text: God is not a man that He should lie, nor a son of man that He should change His mind.
options.note: This is the exact declaration in verse 19.

options.text: God changes His plans according to human sacrifice and ritual.
options.note: The oracle says the opposite, that God does not change His mind.

options.text: God can be persuaded to curse Israel with enough offerings.
options.note: The entire oracle insists that no offering or relocation can reverse God's blessing.

options.text: The oracle makes no statement about God's character.
options.note: Verse 19 is one of the most direct statements of God's character in the passage.

quiz.q: What did Balak suggest after two failed attempts to have Israel cursed?

options.text: That Balaam neither curse nor bless them at all, then took him to yet another location to try again.
options.note: Verses 25 to 28 describe Balak's frustrated suggestion followed by another attempt at Peor.

options.text: That Balaam be paid double and sent home immediately.
options.note: Balak instead took Balaam to a third location, Peor, hoping for a different result.

options.text: That Balak abandon the plan entirely and make peace with Israel.
options.note: Balak persisted in trying to secure a curse rather than abandoning the plan.

options.text: Nothing further is recorded after the second oracle.
options.note: Verses 25 to 30 describe Balak's continued persistence.

quiz.q: What reason did Balaam repeatedly give for why he could not curse Israel, even under pressure?

options.text: He could only speak exactly what the LORD put in his mouth.
options.note: Verses 12 and 26 both restate this same principle.

options.text: He personally admired Israel too much to curse them.
options.note: Balaam frames his inability as obedience to God's word, not personal affection for Israel.

options.text: He feared Israel's army would retaliate against him.
options.note: No such fear is mentioned; his stated reason is fidelity to what God tells him to say.

options.text: No reason is given for his refusal.
options.note: Verses 12 and 26 both give this reason explicitly.

questions: Balak kept relocating Balaam, hoping a new vantage point would change the outcome. Where are you tempted to keep changing your approach rather than accepting that God's word on a matter will not change?
The oracle declares that God is not a man who lies or changes His mind. Where do you struggle to trust that a promise God has made to you is still standing firm?
Balaam insisted he could only speak what God gave him, yet his heart is later revealed to be compromised. Where might your outward words be more faithful than your inward desires right now?

God's blessing on Israel held firm even while Israel themselves were unaware of the danger and the defense happening on their behalf. Where might God be protecting you in ways you cannot currently see?
The passage insists no spell or divination can touch those God has blessed. What fears or forces feel threatening to you right now that this truth might speak directly into?

translationNotes.note: Lifted up an oracle renders a Hebrew idiom, vayisa meshalo, used specifically for solemn, elevated prophetic speech, marking these declarations as formal and weighty rather than casual predictions.
The dust of Jacob likely refers to Israel's uncountable numbers, echoing the promise to Abraham that his offspring would be like the dust of the earth, Genesis 13:16.

Son of man here is a generic Hebrew phrase, ben adam, meaning simply a human being, not a technical messianic title as it later becomes in Daniel and the Gospels; the verse contrasts God's unchanging nature with ordinary human fickleness.
